name: Rollup
summary: A JavaScript module bundler that builds an analyzed module graph through plugin hooks, tree-shakes included statements, and generates one or more output bundles with chunk and code-splitting decisions.

features.name: Plugin-driven module graph
features.description: Rollup's Graph initializes a ModuleLoader and PluginDriver; entries and plugin-emitted entries are loaded, resolved, transformed, parsed, and recursively followed through static and dynamic dependencies. The resulting graph is the input to later analysis and generation.
benefits: Keeps resolution, loading, and transformation extensible
Makes dependency discovery and module ownership explicit
costs: Plugin behavior affects graph completeness and module identity
I/O, parsing, and plugin caches add build coordination cost

features.name: Tree-shaking and execution analysis
features.description: During the build phase Rollup sorts and binds modules, repeatedly marks included statements, and uses AST side-effect analysis to omit statements that are not needed by the output. The fixed architecture document describes this as a distinct phase before chunk rendering.
benefits: Can remove unused statements while preserving analyzed dependencies and side effects
Separates semantic inclusion decisions from output formatting
costs: Side-effect uncertainty limits removal and can retain more code
Repeated inclusion passes add analysis time and require conservative semantics

features.name: Chunk assignment and output generation
features.description: Rollup returns a bundle after graph building; generate and write then create output bundles, assign modules to chunks, render chunks, apply output hooks, and finalize hashes and format-specific wrappers. Multiple outputs can be generated from the same analyzed bundle.
benefits: Reuses graph analysis across output formats
Makes code splitting and output rendering explicit stages
costs: Chunk boundaries and format wrappers affect inter-module semantics
Output configuration and dynamic imports add coordination constraints

features.name: Node, browser, and native/WASM package boundary
features.description: The official architecture documentation distinguishes Node, browser, CLI, native platform packages, and WASM builds. The core JavaScript interface is shared where possible, while file access and native parser/runtime dependencies are adapted at package boundaries.
benefits: Supports multiple host distributions around a common bundling interface
Offers browser and WASM paths where native modules are unavailable
costs: Host capabilities and plugin file-loading requirements differ by package
Publishing platform-specific native artifacts increases release complexity

mathematical_views.question: How do plugin resolution, loading, transformation, parsing, and dependency discovery construct Rollup's graph?
assumptions: Modules and external modules are graph nodes
Plugin hooks define transitions for module identity and source
The view abstracts filesystem and native parser implementation details

mathematical_views.question: Which statements reach the tree-shaken output after repeated inclusion and side-effect analysis?
assumptions: AST nodes expose inclusion and effect observations
The inclusion process reaches a practical fixed point before generation
The model does not claim semantic equivalence for code with unknown side effects

mathematical_views.question: How does one analyzed bundle map to output formats, chunks, rendered assets, and code-splitting boundaries?
assumptions: Build analysis can be reused for multiple output options
Chunk assignment and rendering are separate transformations
File naming, hashes, and format wrappers are output concerns

benefits: Extensible graph construction through ordered hooks
costs: Plugin correctness and cache behavior affect graph validity

benefits: Compact output based on explicit dependency and effect analysis
costs: Conservative side-effect handling can retain code and increase analysis cost

benefits: Multiple output formats and explicit code splitting
costs: Chunk and wrapper decisions can change loading and execution behavior

benefits: Common interface across Node, browser, native, and WASM distributions
costs: Separate host constraints and artifacts increase release surface
